metadata.name: Acute sinusitis (acute rhinosinusitis)
metadata.emergency_level: Routine — mostly viral and self-limiting; rare orbital/intracranial complications are emergencies
metadata.severity: Usually mild-moderate and self-limiting; bacterial cases and complications are less common

overview.short_description: Acute inflammation of the paranasal sinuses and nasal mucosa, usually following a viral cold, presenting with nasal blockage, facial pain/pressure and nasal discharge for less than 12 weeks.
overview.detailed_description: Acute rhinosinusitis is common and mostly viral; only a minority are bacterial. Most cases resolve without antibiotics. Key clinical tasks are to identify the few likely-bacterial cases (persistent >10 days or 'double-sickening'), avoid unnecessary antibiotics, and recognise the rare but serious complications (orbital or intracranial spread).
overview.pathophysiology: Mucosal inflammation and oedema (usually post-viral) obstruct sinus ostia, impairing drainage and mucociliary clearance; secretions stagnate, occasionally allowing secondary bacterial infection (commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis).
overview.etiology: Most commonly viral (as part of a cold). Bacterial superinfection in a minority. Predisposing factors: allergic rhinitis, anatomical variants (deviated septum), dental infection, smoking.
overview.natural_history: Most improve within 2-3 weeks; symptoms worsening after ~5 days or persisting beyond 10 days suggest possible bacterial infection.
overview.prognosis: Excellent; complications are rare. Recurrent/persistent (>12 weeks) becomes chronic rhinosinusitis.

prevalence.value: Very common; many adults have at least one episode yearly, usually viral.

incidence.value: High, peaking in colder months alongside viral URTIs.

mortality.value: Negligible; deaths only via rare intracranial complications.

risk_factors.lifestyle: Recent viral URTI, swimming/diving, air travel.
risk_factors.diabetes: Poor control raises risk of invasive fungal sinusitis (rare, serious).
risk_factors.pregnancy: Not a risk factor; affects medication choice (decongestants).
risk_factors.previous_diseases: Allergic rhinitis, nasal polyps, deviated septum, dental infection (upper molars).

chief_complaints.importance: Purulence alone does not confirm bacterial cause

symptoms.importance: One of the two required features (with discharge or facial pain)

symptoms.symptom: Facial pain/pressure (over sinuses, worse on bending)
Nasal discharge (anterior or postnasal, may be purulent)
symptoms.importance: Colour does not reliably indicate bacterial infection
High fever with severe unilateral pain may suggest bacterial cause

negative_findings.finding: No eye swelling/redness, no diplopia or reduced eye movements, no proptosis
negative_findings.why_important: Absence argues strongly against orbital complications (a key safety check)

negative_findings.finding: No severe headache, neck stiffness, focal neurology, or altered consciousness

negative_findings.why_important: Favours viral (self-limiting) rather than bacterial sinusitis

history_questions.question: How long have symptoms lasted and did they improve then worsen?
history_questions.why_ask: Duration >10 days or double-sickening suggests bacterial cause

history_questions.question: Do you have blocked nose PLUS facial pain/pressure or discharge or reduced smell?
Any eye swelling/redness, double vision, severe headache, or neck stiffness?
History of allergies, nasal polyps, or recurrent sinusitis?
Any recent dental problems in the upper teeth?

physical_examination.expected_finding: Tenderness over sinuses; congested nasal mucosa, discharge

physical_examination.examination: Eyes — periorbital swelling, proptosis, eye movements, vision
physical_examination.expected_finding: Should be normal; abnormality signals orbital complication

vital_signs.temperature: Normal or mild fever (high fever may suggest bacterial cause/complication)

imaging.when_needed: Suspected complications, chronic/recurrent disease, or before surgery
imaging.expected_findings: Sinus opacification; orbital/intracranial extension if complicated

other_diagnostic_tests.endoscopy: Nasal endoscopy by ENT for chronic/recurrent or complicated disease
other_diagnostic_tests.biopsy: Only if malignancy or invasive fungal disease suspected
other_diagnostic_tests.culture: Endoscopically-guided culture in refractory/complicated cases (not routine sinus swab)

diagnostic_criteria.formal_criteria: EPOS: sudden onset of >=2 symptoms, one of which is nasal blockage/obstruction OR nasal discharge (anterior/posterior), +/- facial pain/pressure, +/- reduction/loss of smell, for <12 weeks. Likely BACTERIAL if: symptoms >10 days without improvement, OR severe symptoms/high fever, OR 'double-sickening' (worsening after initial improvement).
diagnostic_criteria.diagnostic_scores: No routine score; clinical criteria (EPOS/NICE) guide viral vs likely-bacterial.

cutoff_values.value: Duration <12 weeks = acute; >12 weeks = chronic rhinosinusitis. >10 days or double-sickening raises bacterial likelihood.

differential_diagnosis.differences: Shorter, no marked localised facial pain, resolves by ~10 days
Itchy eyes/nose, sneezing, seasonal/trigger pattern, no purulence/fever
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Are your nose/eyes itchy and is it triggered by allergens?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Related to upper molar disease, foul unilateral discharge
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Any upper tooth pain or recent dental work?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Eye swelling/proptosis, painful/restricted eye movements, vision change, severe headache, neurology
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_exam: Proptosis, restricted eye movement, focal neurology
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Any eye swelling, double vision, or severe headache?

differential_diagnosis.disease: Migraine / trigeminal or facial pain syndromes
differential_diagnosis.differences: Recurrent, no nasal purulence, migraine features
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Do you get recurrent headaches with light sensitivity rather than nasal symptoms?

diagnostic_questions.question: Have symptoms lasted more than 10 days, or did you improve then get worse?
diagnostic_questions.purpose: Identify likely-bacterial cases for antibiotic consideration

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have any eye swelling, double vision, or a severe headache?

next_best_question.current_situation: Nasal blockage + facial pain, <10 days, well
next_best_question.question: Are your symptoms improving, and do you have any eye or severe headache symptoms?
next_best_question.expected_answers: Improving/no red flags vs persistent/red flags
next_best_question.branching_logic: Improving, no red flags -> symptomatic advice, no antibiotics; >10 days/double-sickening -> consider antibiotics; eye/neuro red flags -> emergency referral

next_best_test.test: Urgent contrast CT/MRI orbit and brain

red_flags.finding: Periorbital swelling, proptosis, painful/restricted eye movements, or reduced/double vision
red_flags.immediate_action: Emergency — same-day ENT/ophthalmology; suspect orbital cellulitis/abscess

red_flags.finding: Severe frontal headache, neck stiffness, focal neurology, or altered consciousness
Systemically very unwell / signs of sepsis
Immunocompromised or poorly-controlled diabetic with severe/necrotic sinusitis

referral_criteria.urgent_referral: Recurrent acute or chronic rhinosinusitis for ENT assessment; unilateral symptoms or unilateral bloody discharge (exclude tumour).
referral_criteria.routine_referral: Persistent symptoms despite treatment; suspected allergic or anatomical cause.
referral_criteria.emergency_referral: Orbital or intracranial complications; suspected invasive fungal sinusitis.

early: Intracranial spread (meningitis, epidural/subdural/brain abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis)

initial_management.supportive_care: Reassurance (most are viral and self-limiting); analgesia; nasal saline irrigation; adequate fluids.
initial_management.medications: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Paracetamol; NSAID; High-dose intranasal corticosteroid; Guideline-directed antibiotic. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: NICE_NG79.
initial_management.lifestyle_advice: Steam inhalation and saline may ease symptoms; smoking cessation; manage underlying allergy.
initial_management.follow_up: Safety-net: return if eye symptoms, severe headache, or no improvement; review recurrent cases.
initial_management.legacy_medications_pre_v13: Symptomatic: analgesia/antipyretics, saline irrigation, short-term decongestants (avoid prolonged use). Intranasal corticosteroid may help symptoms in persistent cases (>10 days). ANTIBIOTICS NOT ROUTINE; reserve for likely-bacterial cases (>10 days without improvement, marked worsening/double-sickening, or systemically very unwell) per NICE NG79.

patient_education.home_advice: Sinus infections are usually caused by viruses and get better within 2-3 weeks without antibiotics. Salt-water rinses, steam, pain relief and decongestants can ease symptoms. See a doctor urgently if you get swelling or redness around an eye, double vision, a severe headache, or a stiff neck.
patient_education.home_advice_ar: التهاب الجيوب غالباً فيروسي ويتحسّن خلال أسبوعين إلى ثلاثة دون مضادات حيوية. غسول الماء والملح والبخار ومسكّنات الألم ومزيلات الاحتقان تخفّف الأعراض. راجع الطبيب فوراً إذا حدث تورّم أو احمرار حول العين، أو ازدواج الرؤية، أو صداع شديد، أو تيبّس الرقبة.
patient_education.prevention: Manage allergic rhinitis, avoid smoking, hand hygiene to reduce colds.
patient_education.warning_signs: Eye swelling/redness, double or reduced vision, severe headache, neck stiffness, or symptoms worsening after 10 days.

prevention.vaccination: No specific vaccine; influenza vaccination reduces some precipitating URTIs.
prevention.lifestyle: Allergy control, smoking cessation, hand hygiene.

evidence.evidence_level: High — most acute sinusitis is viral and self-limiting; antibiotics give limited benefit.
evidence.guideline_strength: The main diagnosis/test and treatment direction was checked against the current guidance identified by NICE_NG79; see evidence_review for scope and limitations. This does not verify every legacy narrative sentence.
